text: The bridge was built in the Old King's day, when roads were laid across the realm; before it there was a ferry.
The stone bridge over {RIVER} has paid for three lords' weddings with its tolls.
The first bridge here was timber and burned in some forgotten war; the stone one is younger than the sept.
Armies have crossed at this ford in every war, so the village keeps its grain in the cellars.
Men have forded {RIVER} here since the First Men; a holdfast on the far bank still takes the toll.
An inn stood at this crossing before the Conquest; its sign has changed with every king.
Wandering septons, singers and hedge knights meet at the crossroads inn on their way to everywhere.
The village grew along the road one alehouse at a time; carters still stop here for the night.
Hedge knights ride this road looking for service, and the village feeds them for their news.
Spring floods once carried off half the houses; the new ones stand on the high bank.
Barges and fishing boats tie up at the landing on {RIVER}; the village has always lived off the water.
Its fishers have worked this shore since before the Andals; the boats are still built the old way.
The village lies among its fields, away from the road, and most wars have passed it by.
Its fields were cleared from the woods by younger sons who could hope for no land at home.
Its boats fish the lake; on still days the far shore seems close enough to touch.
Broken men and outlaws come with every war, and the village has learned to hide its seed corn.
Its oldest families say they were here before the Andals, and the Andals married them anyway.
The village has paid its rents in grain and eggs to {SEAT} for as long as anyone remembers.
Floods, sickness and war have each half emptied the village, and each time it filled again.
First Men cleared these fields; the stones of their old ringfort still lie under the turf.
Its people say their forebears fought for the Kings of Winter long before any dragon came.
In hard winters its people shelter behind the walls of {SEAT} and come home with the thaw.
The old men still say Torrhen Stark knelt to the dragon so that their forefathers would not burn.
Men from the village marched south in Robert's Rebellion; fewer came back from the Trident.
Some of its men sailed with Lord Stark to the siege of Pyke in 289 AC.
A holdfast of the First Men stood here once; only its well and a grassy barrow remain.
Its fields were first given to a younger son of {SEAT}, with a holdfast and the land around it.
A hard winter once took half the village; the dead lie under the cairn on the hill.
The Andals never came north of the Neck, and the old men here are proud of it.
When the Old King's roads were laid, the cattle track past the village became a road.
Riders from {SEAT} change horses here; the stable is older than the stone well.
Two old tracks met here long before the Conquest; the inn at the crossing has had many names.
A lord of {SEAT} built the bridge after the old ford drowned a wedding party.
The ford is passable from spring to the first snows; in winter the river is crossed on the ice.
The village grew where {RIVER} could be crossed in summer and fished in every season.
Its first houses stood on the high bank, above the floods of the spring thaw.
Fishers here have worked the cold sea since the First Men; the boats are still built the old way.
Its fields were won from the wood by axe and fire; the stumps still show at the edges.
The Barrow Kings once ruled here as Kings of the First Men; their mounds still dot the fields.
Under the Red Kings of the Dreadfort its people learned to fear the flayed man; some still do.
Andal ships once came up the Weeping Water; King Theon Stark and the Boltons threw them back.
Many families here came north with the Manderlys, when the Gardener kings drove them from the Reach.
No southern host has ever taken Moat Cailin, and the village has never seen an Andal king.
Crannogmen trade frogs and fish here; their castle moves, they say, and no stranger finds it.
The Starks have held this land since the Age of Heroes, and the village has never known another liege.
In 226 AC its men fought Raymun Redbeard's wildlings at Long Lake beside the Umbers and Lord Willam Stark.
The Umbers have held back wildlings here for centuries, and every house keeps an axe by the door.
The Karstarks are Starks by blood, the village says, and says it proudly.
Ironborn reavers have harried this shore for centuries, and the boats are kept far up the beach.
Brandon's Gift has been farmed for thousands of years to feed the Watch; the village is one of the few left.
Queen Alysanne asked for the New Gift in 58 AC; settlers came then, and wildling raids drove most away.
Wildling raiders cross the Wall every few winters; the village pays its tithe to the Watch and hopes.
In 226 AC Raymun Redbeard's wildlings passed through; the black brothers came too late to help.
The Nightfort was abandoned in the Old King's day; the village keeps well clear of its ruins.
Like Mole's Town, the village lives half under the ground when winter comes.
Every boy here has watched black brothers ride by, and some have taken the black themselves.
The Watch had ten thousand men at the Conquest and has fewer than a thousand now; the village feels it.
Its orchards went wild when the Watch could no longer keep them; the village picks what it can.
Hardhome burned six hundred years ago; old women here say its glow lit the northern sky.
Lords send their criminals to the Wall along this road, and the village feeds them on the way.
Its fields were cleared by settlers of the New Gift; half of them lie fallow now.
When ships come to Eastwatch, they buy salt fish here; most years they do not come.
In the long winters the village shuts its doors and lives on what it salted in autumn.
The black brothers' rangers come back fewer every year, and the village has stopped asking why.
Free folk have lived here since before there was a Wall, and they kneel to no one.
Raymun Redbeard gathered the clans in 226 AC; the village sent men south, and few came back from Long Lake.
Bael the Bard stole a Stark daughter, the songs say, and the village still sings it to annoy the crows.
Hardhome burned six hundred years ago, and no one from the village will camp near its ruins.
Joramun blew the Horn of Winter and woke giants from the earth, the old women say.
Thenns come down from their hidden valley to trade bronze for furs, and keep apart.
Weirwoods still grow thick in the woods here; the free folk say the old gods see everything.
Raiders from the village have crossed the Wall more than once, and come back with southron steel.
Gendel and Gorne led the free folk under the Wall in the old days, the singers say.
Its people are hunters and spearwives; the strongest chief takes what he can hold.
Winters here kill more than any war; every family has lost someone to the snow.
The Frostfangs loom over the village; in summer the clans come down to trade.
Mammoth bones mark the path to the village; the giants passed this way once.
The village sits on {RIVER}, where the clans meet when the hunting is poor.
Slavers from across the sea once took people from this shore, the elders say.
The stoneborn rose against Winterfell in the reign of Daeron II; Lord Barthogan Stark died putting them down.
Traders say the lords of Skagos ride shaggy unicorns; the village does not deny it.
Mainlanders say the Skagosi eat men in winter; the village says mainlanders talk too much.
Skagos is Stark land in name; the village has seen a Stark ship once in living memory.
Ships that pass too close to this coast are said to be lured onto the rocks by false lights.
Some tales blame Skagosi cannibals for the ruin of Hardhome; the village has its own tale.
The stoneborn clans have held these crags since the First Men, and no Andal ever came.
The village lives in stone houses half sunk into the hill, out of the sea wind.
Its clan has feuded with the next valley for longer than anyone can count.
Wildling ships sometimes put in here; the stoneborn trade with them, and fight them.
Seals and whales feed the village in winter, and their oil lights its halls.
The village pays no tax to Winterfell and sends no levies; the Starks have stopped asking.
A weirwood grove above the village is older than any house on the island.
The stoneborn bury their dead in the rock, and do not speak of them to strangers.
Sailors from White Harbor call this coast cursed, and steer wide of it.
First Men raised the first huts here; the Andals came later, with steel and the seven-pointed star.
Under the Storm Kings, and later the ironborn kings, the village paid tribute it never forgot.
Men from the village died in Harren's quarries, chained to the sledges that built Harrenhal.
When Aegon came, Lord Edmyn Tully rose against Harren, and the men of the village rose with him.
In 196 AC its men marched to the Redgrass Field, some for the red dragon and some for the black.
Its men fought on the Trident in 283 AC, though no one here agrees on which side.
After the Trident in 283 AC the village children dived for Rhaegar's rubies; none were ever found.
Barges have carried grain down {RIVER} from this landing since the days of the river kings.
Mummers' carts and wandering septons pass in every season, and the village never lacks for news.
Its fields lie away from the river, too poor to be fought over, and so the village has survived.
On a clear day the Isle of Faces can be seen from the shore; no one rows out there.
In 129 AC Brackens and Blackwoods fought by a burning mill nearby; the feud is older than the mill.
Brackens and Blackwoods have quarrelled over these fields for a thousand years, and both have burned it.
When the bells of Stoney Sept rang in 283 AC, the village hid its people in the cellars.
Its lords swear to Riverrun, where Aegon raised the Tullys over all the riverlands.
Every cart that crosses at the Twins pays the Freys, and the village sells them bread, not love.
In 289 AC ironborn longships came against Seagard, where Lord Jason Mallister slew Rodrik Greyjoy.
The ruined towers of Harrenhal cast long shadows; folk here say the castle is cursed, and many lords agree.
Harren cut weirwoods three thousand years old for his rafters; the village still curses his name.
Harwyn Hardhand won the riverlands at Fairmarket, and the village paid the ironborn for three generations.
Smallfolk here will not climb High Heart at night; the ghosts of the children of the forest walk there.
Salt has been dried in pans along this shore for as long as Saltpans has had its name.
The first Andal ships landed on the Fingers, and the village says its founders came with them.
Since the Andals the Arryns have ruled the Vale, and the village has paid its dues to the Eyrie for thousands of years.
Clansmen from the Mountains of the Moon have raided here in living memory; the knights ride out every spring.
Its men rode under Jon Arryn's banners in 282 AC, when the Vale rose for Robert.
In the Dance of the Dragons the Vale stood for Rhaenyra, and the village sent men and grain.
The Vale shut its roads and ports in 209 AC, and the Great Spring Sickness passed the village by.
The Arryn kings built septs and septries across the Vale; the village sept is one of them.
In 97 AC the Stone Crows killed Lady Jeyne's father and brothers; the village has kept its spears since.
Snowmelt from the Mountains of the Moon floods the river each spring, so the village stands on the high bank.
The valley roads meet here; septons, wool carts and knights pass in every season.
Its fields lie in a fold of the hills, out of sight of the road and of the clansmen.
Every host that tried the Bloody Gate has broken there, and the village has fed the garrison for centuries.
When Jon Arryn took Gulltown from the Graftons in 282 AC, the village quartered his knights.
The Royces of Runestone are older than the Arryns, and their bronze runes are older still.
The Corbrays won the Fingers in the Andal wars, and the village still sings of it.
Its old songs are of the Battle of the Seven Stars, fought at the foot of the Giant's Lance.
Mainlanders call the Sistermen smugglers and wreckers; the village says only that it fishes.
Gold and silver have come out of these hills since the First Men, and the Lannisters have taken their share since Lann.
The Kings of the Rock ruled here until Loren Lannister knelt after the Field of Fire.
When the Andals came, the Lannisters took them in as wards and brides, and the first sept was raised here.
In 261 AC its men marched with young Tywin Lannister against the Reynes of Castamere.
Its people still sing The Rains of Castamere, and know better than to sing it at the wrong table.
Its men marched with Lord Tywin to King's Landing in 283 AC, and some came home richer.
The Red Kraken's longships harried this shore in 130 AC and carried off wives and daughters.
The stream below the village once ran yellow with mine washings, the old women say.
Ore carts and wool carts have worn ruts in this road since the Kings of the Rock.
In 289 AC the village watched the Lannister fleet burn in the harbour of Lannisport.
The Great Spring Sickness of 209 AC came out of Lannisport and took many in the village.
The Golden Tooth guards the pass to the riverlands, and armies have come through it in every war.
The silver workings in the hills above the village are older than any lord's name.
The Banefort watches the sea for ironborn sails, and the village keeps a beacon on the hill.
The Westerlings' gold mines gave out long ago, and the village lives from the sea and the fields now.
The Cleganes won their land when a kennelman saved a Lannister from a lioness; the village remembers the dogs.
Garth Greenhand taught the First Men to sow here, the old songs say, and the soil has never failed since.
The Gardener kings welcomed the Andals with marriages, not swords, and the village took the Seven in peace.
Its men went to the Field of Fire with King Mern in 2 BC, and the dragons burned them there.
When Aegon gave Highgarden to the Tyrells, the village paid its dues to new masters without a battle.
Its men spent a year at the siege of Storm's End in Robert's war, and came home with nothing but stories.
A Gardener king built the first sept here; the Tyrells only gave it a new roof.
Carts of grain and apples roll past {VILLAGE} all autumn, bound for {SEAT}.
Travelling knights, singers and septons meet at the inn here on the way to every tourney.
Its orchards and fields lie off the road, quiet enough that no war has found it in a century.
Barges have carried wine and grain down {RIVER} from this landing since the Gardener kings.
Ironborn longships raided this coast in the old days, until the Gardener kings armed the Shield Islands.
In 130 AC the Two Betrayers burned Tumbleton with dragonfire, and the village took in what was left.
Ormund Hightower's host was trapped on the Honeywine in 130 AC, a day's ride from here.
Before the Field of Fire, Loren and Mern joined their hosts at Goldengrove, and the village fed both kings.
At Ashford in 282 AC Lord Tarly broke Robert Baratheon's van before Mace Tyrell even arrived.
The Great Spring Sickness of 209 AC was worse in Oldtown than anywhere but King's Landing.
Acolytes of the Citadel walk out here to study the soil and the stars, and pay for their ale.
Horn Hill guards the Dornish marches, and Dornish raiders have burned the village more than once.
The Shield Islands were armed against ironborn reavers, and the village keeps its boats ready.
The Florents say Highgarden should have been theirs, and the village hears it at every harvest feast.
The Oakhearts of Old Oak are older than the Tyrells, and the village never lets anyone forget it.
Its people send grain and roses to Highgarden, as they did when green-crowned kings sat there.
The Storm Kings ruled here from Storm's End for thousands of years; its walls, they say, were raised by Bran the Builder.
Its men followed Argilac the Arrogant to the Last Storm, where Orys Baratheon slew him.
In 282 AC Robert won three battles in one day at Summerhall, and men from here fought in all three.
It rains here more than anywhere in the realm, the villagers boast, and their mossy roofs agree.
In the Dance of the Dragons the storm lords followed Lord Borros Baratheon for Aegon II.
When Lyonel Baratheon, the Laughing Storm, crowned himself Storm King, the village sent him its sons.
Arlan III led the storm lords north and took the riverlands, and the village's forefathers went with him.
{RIVER} floods with the autumn rains, and the village has learned to build on the high ground.
Storms off the narrow sea wreck ships every autumn, and the village salvages what the sea gives.
The Kingswood Brotherhood robbed travellers on this road until the Kingsguard broke them in 281 AC.
The Last Storm was fought near Bronzegate in 2 BC, and ploughs here still turn up rusted helms.
During the year-long siege of Storm's End the Reach host ate the village bare.
Dornish raiders came over the mountains for a thousand years, and every house here has a hiding cellar.
Summerhall burned in 259 AC and the king died with it; the village saw the glow from its fields.
In the First Dornish War Lord Fowler came over the mountains and burned Nightsong.
The Selmys of Harvest Hall gave the realm Ser Barristan the Bold, and every boy here has fought him with a stick.
The Rainwood begins behind the last field, and outlaws and ghosts are both said to live there.
Aegon landed at the mouth of the Blackwater in 2 BC, and the lords hereabouts were among the first to kneel.
Its people have seen Targaryen and Baratheon kings ride past, and paid the same taxes to both.
In the Dance of the Dragons the city changed hands more than once, and the village fed whoever held it.
The Old King's roads were begun in 62 AC, and the village grew up beside one of them.
The Kingswood Brotherhood robbed travellers on this road until the Kingsguard broke them in 281 AC.
Barges come down the Blackwater Rush to the city, and the village sells them bread and eels.
Its fishers sell crabs and eels in the city's markets, and the walk there takes all night.
Its fields have fed the capital since Aegon's day, and the tax-men know every furrow.
Queen Rhaenys flew to Rosby in the Conquest, and Rosby yielded without a fight.
In 277 AC King Aerys was held captive in Duskendale for half a year, and the village paid for the Defiance.
The Darklyns once ruled from Duskendale as kings; after the Defiance not one of them was left.
The Great Spring Sickness of 209 AC killed four in ten in King's Landing; the village buried its dead in the fields.
When the Lannisters sacked King's Landing in 283 AC, refugees filled the village for a month.
In 130 AC a mob stormed the Dragonpit, and the village saw the fires from its fields.
The lords hereabouts have sent their sons to court for three hundred years, and their debts home.
The Targaryens came to Dragonstone before the Doom, and these lands have served dragons ever since.
Dragons flew over this coast in the Dance of the Dragons, and the village still tells of fire in the sky.
After Robert's war the last Targaryen ships left Dragonstone, and Stannis Baratheon came to rule it.
In 130 AC the Triarchy's fleet sacked Spicetown on Driftmark, and the village still fears sails from the east.
Storms off the narrow sea take a boat from the village every year; the widows keep the count.
Riders bound for King's Landing water their horses here, and leave their news behind.
The Crackclaws are First Men blood; no Andal king ever conquered them, and they remind visitors of it.
Blood feuds run deep here; two families of the village have not spoken since before the Conquest.
In 129 AC Princess Rhaenys and her dragon Meleys fell in battle at Rook's Rest, close by.
Lord Fell rode to Summerhall in 282 AC and died there by Robert's hand; the village mourned him.
The Celtigars came from Valyria with the Targaryens, and the village serves them as it always has.
Its lord was once a smuggler who carried onions to Storm's End during the siege.
The drowned men say the Grey King himself once walked this shore.
In the Old Way its men paid the iron price on every coast of the Sunset Sea.
Thralls taken in raids tilled this thin soil while the ironborn went reaving.
Its longships sailed with Harwyn Hardhand when the ironborn won the riverlands.
When Harrenhal burned in 2 BC, the village lost sons who had gone east with Harren.
After Harren burned, the ironborn chose Vickon Greyjoy to rule them, and the village gave him its oars.
In 130 AC its longships followed the Red Kraken to sack Lannisport.
The dragon kings forbade the Old Way; the village grumbled and went fishing, mostly.
Seven families in ten fish here, as the maesters wrote; the other three reave.
The fields are thin and stony; what grows here grows because thralls broke their backs over it.
Each island once had a rock king and a salt king; the village remembers serving both.
Its people despise the gold price; what a man has not taken with iron is not truly his.
The Iron Fleet took men from the village every summer of Balon's rebellion in 289 AC.
Driftwood shelters of the drowned men stand on the beach below the village.
In 289 AC King Robert's knights landed on these islands to end Balon's rebellion.
Lonely Light lies far out in the western sea; the Farwynds, men say, can take the shape of seals.
No ironborn of the village was ever buried on land; they are all given back to the sea.
Its men still tell of the kingsmoot on Old Wyk, where the first High King was chosen.
Nymeria's Rhoynar came ashore about seven hundred years before the Conquest, and their blood runs in the village.
When Nymeria burned her ships, the Rhoynar stayed; their customs still rule inheritance here.
Dorne never knelt to Aegon; in the First Dornish War the village hid in the hills while dragons burned the castles.
The Young Dragon conquered Dorne in 158 AC and lost it within three years; the village saw both.
Dorne joined the realm by marriage in 187 AC, not by the sword, and the village is proud of it.
Prince Lewyn Martell led Dornish spears to the Trident in 283 AC, and few came back to the village.
In Dorne water is worth more than gold, and the lords of the wells fought over this one for centuries.
Caravans cross the deep sand to the village wells, and the well-keeper is the richest man here.
Everything green here lives off {RIVER}; the wells were dug and guarded before any castle.
Orphans of the Greenblood pole their rafts past the village, still mourning Mother Rhoyne.
The salt Dornishmen of this coast trade with Lys and Tyrosh as readily as with the realm.
The bridge spans a river half dry in summer; travellers mock it until the floods come.
The road follows the old caravan track from well to well, and the village is one of the wells.
Its fields are watered by little canals; whoever cuts a neighbour's channel answers for it with blood.
Andal adventurers carved out petty kingdoms here long before Nymeria; the village served three of them.
The sun is the village's oldest enemy; work stops at noon and begins again at dusk.
Dornishmen avoid pitched battle; when armies came, the village went into the hills and waited.
Queen Rhaenys and her dragon Meraxes fell at Hellholt in 10 AC; the village still tells it as a victory.
In the First Dornish War Lord Fowler rode out of Skyreach and burned Nightsong across the mountains.
Dornish raiders rode north through the passes from here for centuries, and stormlanders rode south to repay them.
The Martells have ruled here since Mors Martell wed Nymeria, and the village has known no other princes.
Nymeria's fleet made landfall at the mouth of the Greenblood, within sight of this shore.
The Daynes of Starfall keep a sword forged from a fallen star, the village swears, and so do the singers.
The Yronwoods were kings before the Martells, and the village has not quite forgotten it.
The lemon trees of Lemonwood drink from canals older than the Conquest.
The road past the village is Valyrian, fused stone that has not cracked in a thousand years.
An old Valyrian milestone stands at the crossroads; the distances on it are to cities long gone.
The bridge is Valyrian work, older than the Doom, and no one here knows how it was made.
A toll-keeper of {SEAT} sits at the bridge; even beggars pay to cross.
Caravans cross {RIVER} at this ford in the dry season; in the floods they wait, and spend.
Caravans from three cities meet at this crossroads, and the village lives by their thirst.
Sellswords on the march stop here for water and wine, and the village keeps its daughters indoors.
River galleys and poleboats pass the village landing every day, bound for the sea.
The river floods every spring; the fields are richer for it, and the houses stand on mounds.
Its fishers and smugglers know every cove on this shore; the customs men of {SEAT} know a few.
The village lies off the road among its fields; tax-men are its only regular visitors.
The village paid its dues to Valyria before the Doom and pays {SEAT} now; the sum is about the same.
In the Century of Blood after the Doom, wars and khalasars swept these lands, and the village was burned and built again.
In 96 AC Myr, Lys and Tyrosh joined as the Kingdom of the Three Daughters to clear the Stepstones of pirates.
The Golden Company has fought over these fields in many wars since its founding in 212 AC.
Sellswords of the free companies winter here between wars; the village feeds them and counts the spoons.
Slaves work these fields, three for every free man, as everywhere in the Quarrelsome Daughters.
Andals once tilled these lands, before they took ship for Westeros; their old stones still stand.
Braavos was founded by slaves who fled their Valyrian masters and hid in the fog of the lagoon.
Its families still keep the masks and the ten days of the Uncloaking of Uthero every year.
No man may be a slave in the lands of Braavos, and the village is proud that free hands work its fields.
Braavos and Pentos fought six wars in two hundred years, and the village sent oarsmen to every one.
Moonsingers led the founders to the lagoon, and the village shrine still sings their hymns.
Its young men go to the city to learn the water dance, and come back with scars and stories.
Pine from the hills above the village went to build the war galleys of the Arsenal.
The village has never seen a dragon; the fog that hid Braavos hid it too.
Its fishers row their catch to the fishmongers of Braavos before dawn.
The Iron Bank will have its due, the villagers say, and so will the Sealord's tax-farmers.
On a still night the shepherds swear they hear the Titan of Braavos roar from the sea.
Silver from the hills behind the village paid for many Braavosi ships.
Braavos forbade Pentos its slaves, but the village's bond servants wear collars all the same.
When khalasars come west, the magisters pay them off, and the village pays the magisters.
In the war that ended in 209 AC, Pentos sacrificed four princes in one year, and the village lost its sons.
Braavosi raiders burned the village in one of the six wars, and it was built again in Pentoshi stone.
The magisters' estates swallowed the village fields long ago; most here work another man's land.
Khal Drogo's khalasar camped outside the city in 298 AC, and the village hid its horses.
The ruins of Ghoyan Drohe on the Little Rhoyne, burned by Valyrian dragons, lie a day's walk away.
Its cheeses and wine go to Pentos by cart, and the magisters' tax-men count every wheel.
Pentos may keep no army by Braavosi treaty, so the village keeps its own spears.
Norvos was founded by bearded priests who left Valyria to keep their faith, and the village keeps it too.
The three bells of Norvos rule the day; the village rises and rests by them, as the priests command.
Its terraced fields climb the hills, as they have since the city was young.
Dothraki riders have come into the hills of Norvos before, and the village walls remember them.
The Noyne carries the village's wine down to the Rhoyne and on to Volantis.
The bearded priests choose the magisters, and the magisters choose the tax-men; the village pays them all.
Its sons go to the city to learn the long axe; one of them, they say, now guards a prince of Dorne.
The ruins of Ny Sar, Nymeria's city, destroyed by the dragonlords, lie close by.
Four centuries ago three thousand Unsullied held off Khal Temmo's riders; without them there would be no village.
Qohorik smiths can rework Valyrian steel, and the village sells them charcoal and iron.
The forest of Qohor begins at the village fields, and its woodsmen fell timber for the city.
Every day a beast is given to the Black Goat; in hard years the village gives its best bullock.
Khalasars still ride to the edge of the forest; the village watches the eastern grass every summer.
Rafts of timber float down {RIVER} from the village to the Rhoyne.
The ruins of Ar Noy, a Rhoynish city burned by Valyria, lie upriver of the village.
When Qohor is threatened, its nobles give their own children to the Black Goat; the village gives its prayers.
Mazemakers raised the stone mazes here long before men knew their name, and left no word of why.
Followers of the Blind God settled Lorath from Valyria; their cult is long dead, but their maze-towns remain.
Lorath is the poorest of the Free Cities; the village is poorer still, and does not complain.
Freed and runaway slaves have settled here for centuries, and no one asks a newcomer whose he was.
The Shivering Sea is cold and full of fish, and the village has never gone hungry in summer.
Ibbenese whalers put in here for water and trouble, and the village sells them both.
Refugees from fallen Sarnor passed through in the Century of Blood, the old songs say.
The followers of Boash held all life equal, lord and beggar, man and beast; the village has not forgotten.
The Axe stretches north of the village, and once it was the land of the Andals.
Myr has fought Lys and Tyrosh over the Disputed Lands for centuries, and the village has changed hands often.
In the Daughters' War the Myrmen lost the most, and the village paid for it in sons and grain.
Myrish lace and lenses are made in the city; the flax and the thread come from villages like this.
The red temple of Myr takes boys from villages like this; Thoros of Myr was one of them.
The Sorrows and drowned Chroyane lie near; men who breathe the mist there, they say, turn to stone.
Prince Garin called down his curse on the Valyrians at Chroyane, and the village still makes a sign against it.
Tyrosh grew rich on a sea snail whose dye the dragonlords loved, and the snails are gathered on these shores.
Tyrosh was a Valyrian military outpost before it was a city, and the village still musters spears for the Archon.
Its pear orchards press the brandy Tyrosh sells across the world.
Tyroshi dye their beards in bright colours, and in the village even old men wear green or blue.
Tyrosh has fought Myr and Lys over the Disputed Lands, and the village sits where their borders shift.
The Archon's tax-men come twice a year, and the village hides its brandy once.
Pirates of the Stepstones have raided this shore since the Three Daughters failed to keep them down.
Lys was a pleasure isle of the dragonlords before the Doom, and its masters still live as if it were.
Here too many have the pale hair and violet eyes of old Valyria.
In the Century of Blood the tigers of Volantis ruled Lys for two generations, and the village paid them.
The tears of Lys are a poison; the village grows nothing but grapes and olives, everyone insists.
Lyseni galleys put in at the village for water on their way to the Summer Sea.
Lys fought Myr and Tyrosh over the Disputed Lands, and the village sent spears and grain.
Pleasure barges from Lys drift past the village coast on summer nights.
Volantis was the First Daughter of Valyria, and the village has served the Old Blood since before the Doom.
After the Doom the tigers of Volantis went to war for Valyria's empire, and many of the village's men never came home.
For centuries now the elephants have ruled Volantis, and the village sells to merchants, not to armies.
Five slaves to every free man work these fields, and their faces bear the tattoos of their trade.
Volantis lost a whole fleet in the Smoking Sea trying to reclaim Valyria; the widows' songs are still sung here.
The Black Walls of Volantis keep the Old Blood in and everyone else out; no one from the village has been inside.
The Rhoyne carries the village's grain to Volantis, and river galleys pass every day.
Prince Garin of Chroyane won his first battles near here, a thousand years ago, before the dragons crushed him.
Rhoynish Sar Mell stood here before the dragonlords burned it; its stones are in every village wall.
The Doom fell on Valyria four hundred years ago, and ash still turns up under the plough.
The old Valyrian roads still run straight through the village, though no dragonlord has used them in centuries.
Sailors say the Smoking Sea is cursed, and no one here will sail toward the old Freehold.
Dragonglass still washes up on the shore after storms, and the village sells it to the traders.
Dragonlords once ruled from here; now Volantenes, Ghiscari and outlaws fight over what is left.
The Fourteen Flames still smoke on clear days, and the village prays they stay asleep.
Its people say they descend from the dragonlords' slaves, the only ones who were far enough away.
Treasure-seekers come through every year bound for the ruins; few come back.
The demon road runs near here; travellers who take it rarely come back the same.
Fishers here will not take their boats past the headland, where the water steams.
The soil here is black and rich from the old ash, and strange things grow in it.
The village is built of Valyrian fused stone, cut from the ruins nearby.
Before the Doom the Freehold ruled half the world; the village now rules a field and a well.
Old Ghis fell to the dragonlords five thousand years ago, and the Valyrians sowed its fields with salt.
Slaves work the estates here for masters in {SEAT}; few free men own any land.
Its masters trace their blood to Old Ghis, and wear tokars to prove it.
The harpy of Ghis is carved over the village gate, as over every slaver city.
Dothraki sell their captives in the markets of Slaver's Bay, and the road past the village carries them.
The brown Skahazadhan feeds the village fields before it reaches Meereen.
The slaver cities were Ghiscari colonies long before Valyria took them, and the village fields have known masters ever since.
Overseers with whips walk the village fields; the slaves sing to keep the rhythm.
The Good Masters of the cities quarrel endlessly, and the village pays whoever wins.
Astapor trains its Unsullied from boyhood, and the village has sold boys to the Good Masters.
Yunkai's Wise Masters trade in slaves of every kind, and the village grows their grain.
The pyramids of Meereen can be seen from the hills, and the fighting pits are the village's only holiday.
Mantarys lies at the end of the demon road; travellers from the west arrive frightened or not at all.
The Lamb Men of Lhazar herd sheep here, and every few years the Dothraki come to take slaves.
The Lhazareen say all men are one flock; the Dothraki do not agree.
Qarth is the greatest city that ever was or will be, the Qartheen say, and the village sells it fruit and flowers.
The village wells were dug by order of the ancient kings of Qarth, and are still guarded.
The red waste lies west of here, and whoever crosses it is lucky to see the village.
The warlocks of the House of the Undying are feared here more than any lord.
Qarth sits on the Jade Gates between two seas, and ships from Yi Ti pass the village coast.
The Pureborn trace their blood to the ancient kings of Qarth, and the village pays their taxes.
The Thirteen buy the village's harvest before it is grown, and sell it twice over.
Spice caravans from the east rest here before the last day's march to the city.
The warlocks drink shade of the evening, and their lips are blue; the village children run from them.
Its fishers keep to the coast; the open sea beyond the Jade Gates belongs to the great ships.
Every traveller on this road is going to Qarth or coming back poorer.
The Qartheen weep easily, the traders say, but the village tax-men never do.
Water is carried from the city cisterns to the village in dry years, at a price.
Dothraki never come so far; it is the desert the village fears, not the khals.
The Tourmaline Brotherhood and the Thirteen quarrel in the city; the village keeps its head down.
Its gardens are watered by hand, a bucket at a time, as they have been for a thousand years.
Khalasars ride past each summer, and the village pays in horses and grain, or burns.
Vaes Dothrak lies far to the east beneath the Mother of Mountains, and the riders go there to honour the horse god.
The village stands on the stones of a town the Dothraki burned in the Century of Blood.
Its people are slaves and freedmen who keep horses for a khal; they belong to no khalasar.
The Dothraki take what they want and call it a gift; the village has learned to give first.
Stolen gods line the godsway of Vaes Dothrak; one of them, the old men say, came from this village.
The dosh khaleen of Vaes Dothrak send word through the grass, and every khal listens.
The riders water their horses at {RIVER} below the village, and leave when the grass is gone.
No Dothraki will cross the poison water of the sea, and the village is glad of it.
Twice in living memory two khalasars met here and fought; the bones are still in the grass.
The stallion who mounts the world will come one day, the riders say; the village hopes he passes by.
The grass sea runs to the edge of sight in every direction, and the village is a stone in it.
Lhazareen captives built the first houses here, and their children still herd sheep on the hill.
Traders from the Free Cities come with gifts for the khal, and buy what the village has.
Its fields are small and fenced with stone, so the horses of the khalasars do not graze them bare.
The Tall Men ruled this land until the Dothraki burned their cities in the Century of Blood.
At the Field of Crows the Sarnori host died, and the village was founded by the few who fled.
Saath is all that is left of Sarnor; the village pays it taxes and honours its hundred gods.
Its people still call themselves Tagaez Fen, the Tall Men, though few are tall.
Ruins of a Sarnori city stand on the plain, and the village takes its stone from them.
Sarnath was put to the torch by Khal Loso; the village keeps one of its carved stones over the door.
Once Sarnor ruled all the lands of the Sarne; now the village rules a well and a few fields.
The Sarne still runs past the village as it did when Sarnor had kings.
The Dothraki ride past and burn what is left every few years; the village rebuilds lower each time.
Old men here still remember the names of the Sarnori kings, a hundred names and more.
The lakes here were once the Silver Sea, the old songs say.
Scythed chariots once rode from here against the khals; their wheels lie rusting in the barns.
Traders from Lorath buy the village furs and sell it salt.
Its fields are small and walled with ruins; the rest of the plain belongs to the grass.
No khal has ever kept a promise to the village, and the village has stopped asking for one.
Ibbenese whalers sail from here into the Shivering Sea, and the village smells of whale oil all year.
Ibbenese traders say their islands were old when Valyria was young, and no one here argues.
Ibben was ruled by a God-King until the Doom; now the Shadow Council and the Thousand rule.
Its people are short, broad and hairy, and proud of all three.
Whale-oil lamps hang on iron chains in the village street, as in the Port of Ibben.
The Thousand chose the village's lord, and the village paid for the choosing.
Fat-bellied whalers with tarred hulls are built on the beach below the village.
Ibbenese settlers came over the sea to these mainland hills, and the forest has fought them ever since.
Its men go to sea for a year at a time, and the women run the village.
Dothraki once rode up to the village palisade, looked at it, and rode away.
The forests here are full of pigs and wolves; the village eats the first and fears the second.
Lorathi and Braavosi traders buy the village's oil and amber.
Winter comes early here; the village lays in salt meat before the first frost.
Its fields are cleared from the forest, and the stumps are older than the village.
The only road runs from the village to the harbour, and everything that matters travels on it.
The Port of Ibben is grey and gloomy, the villagers say, and they visit it as rarely as they can.
The God-on-Earth ruled the Great Empire of the Dawn for ten thousand years, the priests of Yin say.
Yi Ti's emperors come and go; the village pays its taxes to whichever one is reigning.
The Bloodstone Emperor brought the Long Night, the Yi Tish tales say, and the village lights lamps at dusk.
The priestly scribes of Yin keep the village in their tax rolls, and have for a thousand years.
Traders from the Jade Sea buy the village's timber and furs for silk.
The forest here is old and dark, and the village keeps to its edge.
Its people burn incense to the Maiden-Made-of-Light every dawn.
Bandits from the hills raid the village roads, and the emperor's soldiers come too late.
The village is far from any emperor, and likes it that way.
Traders say the Church of Starry Wisdom began in Yi Ti; the village says nothing about it.
Its people have seen men from the west only twice, and both times they were lost.
The emperor's road passes the village, but the emperor never has.
Timber rafts float down the river from the village to the sea.
Its fields are terraced up the hillside, a step for every generation.
The Lion of Night is feared here as much as he is worshipped.
Swan ships from the village have sailed as far as Oldtown, and come back with tales of snow.
Summer Islanders sail swan ships across the world, and the village sends its sons as archers.
Their laws are written on the talking trees, and the village keeps its own beneath one.
Goldenheart bows are the best in the world, and the village cuts the wood for them.
Every islander serves a time in the temples of love, and the village is proud of its priests.
Swan ships with white sails put in at the village bay on their way to Oldtown and Qarth.
Silver from the hills here buys the feathers and fruit of the other islands.
Islanders seldom fight in war; when they must, they meet at a holy place and settle it there.
The village wears feathered cloaks on feast days, as its grandmothers did.
Slavers have come to these shores before, and the village keeps its archers ready.
Its people trade spices and fruit for western cloth and steel.
The village bay is blue and deep, and swan ships anchor there in the storm season.
Red archers of the swan ships learn to shoot here, before they ever see a sail.
Its elders say the islands were born of the sea, and will go back to it one day.
Its gardens grow fruit that the west has no names for.
The village honours the god and goddess of love before every voyage.
